rule: bad: an indefinite singular subject with a plain verb makes the translator read this as one particular crowd on one occasion, so you get a standalone fact and no rule at all — nothing fires later when a crowd is described, and the general claim this rule field is meant to state is lost. Rewrite it as an explicit occurrence conditional: 'Whenever a crowd of nightmoths gathers, it brings sky-cats down.'
texts: mixed: the conditional shape is right and fireable — the lantern-row location, the descent and the cliff-spire source are all carried and tied to the gathering — but 'many' has nowhere to go, since the instruction set treats it as a proportion word that sets a strength rather than counts things, so it ends up as a premise condition that an ordinary sentence about moths gathering will never produce and the rule stays matchable only in theory. Use a phrase that counts: 'When a crowd of nightmoths gathers at a lantern-row, sky-cats descend from the cliff-spires.'

bad: 'many' is dropped out of the rule itself — the trigger fires on a SINGLE nightmoth crowding a lantern-row, so the parse claims one moth is enough to bring the sky-cats down, and the quantity survives only in a side atom that restates a range nothing else in the parse quantifies. Give the trigger a countable collective subject: 'If a crowd of nightmoths crowds a lantern-row, sky-cats descend from the cliff-spires.'

mixed: the rule fires and the staying-on-the-spires response is correctly tied to the gathering, but bare 'few' hits the same dead end as 'many' in the previous sentence — a proportion word routed to strength, so it lands as a premise condition no ordinary gathering sentence will emit. Use a counting phrase instead: 'When a handful of nightmoths gather at a lantern-row, sky-cats stay on the cliff-spires.'
